```

We can see this pattern exemplified when looking at correlations between forager movement (*mean.fm*) and the highest vegetation types (*veg_7*, *veg_6*, *veg_5*), that is those that provide the most resources. We generally see negative correlations with the high vegetation types (Figure S\@ref(fig:mobility-veg-correlations)), indicating that low forager mobility is significantly correlated with higher proportions of these vegetation types. 

We can also see that low forager mobility is highly correlated with dispersion of vegetation types, as is evidenced by the positive correlation between *mean.fm* and *veg_morans.i*. This indicates that local heterogeneity of the landscape affects how far the foragers need to move. 

## Correlations between forager mobility and population density

Because mobility is the behavior that agents can control in the model, we looked at how changes in this behavior changes with population evolution using Spearman's rank correlations within climatic intervals. Because there is relatively little change in forager steps within climatic intervals, we looked at the relationship between the starting number of steps during a climatic interval and the resulting population density at the end of that interval. 

```{r mobility-pop-correlations-1, fig.cap="Relationship between average steps per foraging bout during climatic intervals and the resulting population density during the same climatic interval for model scenarios with short climatic cycles (100 ticks)", echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width='100%'}
ggplot(rates %>% 
         filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "100") %>%
         filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps, 
                 color = climate.condition)) +
  # geom_smooth(aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps), 
  #             method = "lm") +
  stat_cor(mapping = aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps), 
           method = "spearman", p.accuracy = 0.01, r.accuracy = 0.01, 
           size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ tick.range, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 6), 
        legend.position = "bottom", 
        strip.text = element_text(size = 7))

```

Throughout model run, these outputs are highly negatively correlated (Figure S\@ref(fig:mobility-pop-correlations-1)). This suggests that lower amounts of mobility allow higher population densities because each foraging group requires less room to meet their foraging needs.

# Forager interactions

When looking at forager interactions, we have to consider them in relation to populations since more foragers on the landscape will necessarily mean more possible interactions. The model outputs interaction counts averaged across all agents and we divided this by the population count to get the average proportion of the population that an individual agent interacts with each tick.

```{r adj-fi-viz, fig.cap="Trends in average proportion of population a given agent interacts with across model run", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.height=7}
ggplot(data %>% filter(ticks > 0)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = ticks, y = adj.fi, color = `movement-model`), se = T) +
  facet_grid(`cycle-duration` + `veg-cycle-start` ~ `burn-cost`, 
             labeller = labeller(`veg-cycle-start` = start.labs, 
                                 `cycle-duration` = cycle.labs, 
                                 `burn-cost` = bc.labs)) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 6))

```

When we visualize these differences (Figure S\@ref(fig:adj-fi-viz)), we can see that for random walks, there is a steep drop off in forager interactions within approximately the first 500 ticks of the model. This is likely because populations are relatively small at the beginning of model run, so each interaction will necessarily be a greater proportion. 

We used Beta regressions to examine the effects of the parameters on the proportion of forager interactions at model tick = 1000 and at the end of model run. To assess the relevance of parameters to the model, we calculate whether each term improved model fit using a LRT test and by calculating the change in likelihood (delatLogLik).

## Forager interactions at the beginning of model run

```{r adj-fi-reg-1, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width='100%', fig.height=3}
reg.params = c(
  "cycle-duration", 
  "veg-distribution",
  "veg-cycle-start", 
  "burn-cost",
  "burn-veg-type-threshold",
  "burnt-neighbor-limit", 
  "movement-model"
)

beta.data1000 = data %>% filter(ticks == 1000) %>%
  mutate(adj.fi = ifelse(adj.fi == 0, adj.fi + 0.00001, adj.fi)) %>% 
  mutate(adj.fi = ifelse(adj.fi == 1, adj.fi - 0.00001, adj.fi)) %>% 
  select_at(c("ticks", "adj.fi", reg.params)) %>%
  mutate(across(reg.params, as.factor))

beta.fit1 = betareg(adj.fi ~ (`cycle-duration` + 
                                `veg-cycle-start` +
                                `veg-distribution` + 
                                `burn-cost` +
                                `burn-veg-type-threshold` + 
                                `burnt-neighbor-limit` + 
                                `movement-model`)^2, 
                    data = beta.data1000, na.action = na.fail)

summary(beta.fit1)$pseudo.r.squared
plot(fitted(beta.fit1), residuals(beta.fit1, type = "pearson"))

terms = attr(terms(beta.fit1), "term.labels")
drop_stats = map_df(terms, function(t) {
  f = as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", t))
  mod_drop = update(beta.fit1, f)
  
  lr = lmtest::lrtest(mod_drop, beta.fit1)
  data.frame(
    term = t,
    LR_stat = lr[2,"Chisq"], 
    p_value = lr[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 
    delatLogLik = as.numeric(logLik(beta.fit1) - logLik(mod_drop))
  )
})

print(drop_stats %>% filter(p_value < 0.05))


```

We can see that, for the early parts of model run (tick = 1000), there are only 7 parameters or interactions for which dropping the term would significantly reduce model fit.  

```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi-1,  out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

print(head(drop_stats[order(-drop_stats$delatLogLik), ] %>% select(term, delatLogLik), n = 10))

```

When we order by the raw improvement in likelihood, we can see that the interactions between burning costs/limits and movement models contribute the most to explaining the variation in the response (have a stronger impact on model fit). 

```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi-2,  out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

as.data.frame(emmeans(beta.fit1, ~ `burn-cost`:`movement-model`) %>%
                pairs(adjust = "tukey")) %>% filter(p.value < 0.05) %>% select(contrast, estimate)

```

When we do pairwise comparisons among the parameter values with Tukey adjustment we can see that most of the significant differences occur with directed walks, where directed walks result in more interaction than random walks. These effect sizes are very small, likely because the interaction proportions themselves are small. We also see that increased burning costs within a particular movement model (here only directed walks) also increase the interaction proportions at the beginning of model run.

## Forager interactions at the end of model run

```{r adj-fi-reg-2, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width='100%', fig.height=3}
reg.params = c(
  "cycle-duration", 
  "veg-distribution",
  "veg-cycle-start", 
  "burn-cost",
  "burn-veg-type-threshold",
  "burnt-neighbor-limit", 
  "movement-model"
)

beta.data3500 = data %>% filter(ticks == 3500) %>%
  mutate(adj.fi = ifelse(adj.fi == 0, adj.fi + 0.00001, adj.fi)) %>% 
  mutate(adj.fi = ifelse(adj.fi == 1, adj.fi - 0.00001, adj.fi)) %>% 
  select_at(c("ticks", "adj.fi", reg.params)) %>%
  mutate(across(reg.params, as.factor))

beta.fit1 = betareg(adj.fi ~ (`cycle-duration` + 
                                `veg-cycle-start` +
                                `veg-distribution` + 
                                `burn-cost` +
                                `burn-veg-type-threshold` + 
                                `burnt-neighbor-limit` + 
                                `movement-model`)^3, 
                    data = beta.data3500, na.action = na.fail)

summary(beta.fit1)$pseudo.r.squared
plot(fitted(beta.fit1), residuals(beta.fit1, type = "pearson"))

terms = attr(terms(beta.fit1), "term.labels")
drop_stats = map_df(terms, function(t) {
  f = as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", t))
  mod_drop = update(beta.fit1, f)
  
  lr = lmtest::lrtest(mod_drop, beta.fit1)
  data.frame(
    term = t,
    LR_stat = lr[2,"Chisq"], 
    p_value = lr[2, "Pr(>Chisq)"], 
    delatLogLik = as.numeric(logLik(beta.fit1) - logLik(mod_drop))
  )
})

print(head(drop_stats[order(-drop_stats$delatLogLik), ] %>% select(term, delatLogLik), n = 10))

```
For forager interactions at the end of model run we again see that the interactions between movement models and burning rules are of high importance for explaining variation. We can also see that the ending vegetation productivity state (determined by the *cycle-duration* and *veg-cycle-start* interaction) affects forager interactions, likely because of the effect this has on mobility. Interestingly, we also see the underlying vegetation distribution included in these important interactions. 

```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi-3,  out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

as.data.frame(emmeans(beta.fit1, ~ `veg-distribution`) %>%
                pairs(adjust = "tukey")) %>% filter(p.value < 0.05) %>% select(contrast, estimate)

```

When we look at the pairwise comparisons on vegetation distribution, we see that landscapes with clustered underlying vegetation structure result in more interactions than landscapes with no imposed underlying vegetation structure. 


```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi-4,  out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

as.data.frame(emmeans(beta.fit1, ~ `burn-cost`:`movement-model`) %>%
                pairs(adjust = "tukey")) %>% filter(p.value < 0.05) %>% select(contrast, estimate)

```

This vegetation distribution effect interacts with those of burning costs/limits and movement models as well. When we look at the two way interaction of burning costs and movement models, we see that directed walks result in more interaction unless burning costs are high. Increased burning costs also results in more interactions regardless of movement model.

## Change in forager interactions over time
```{r interaction-change-over-time, fig.cap="Change in proportion of the population foragers interact with across each climatic interval", out.width="100%", fig.height=6, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(rates %>% 
         filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "250")) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = tick.range, y = interactions.slope, 
                   color = climate.condition)) +
  facet_grid( `movement-model` ~ `burn-cost`, 
              scales = "free", labeller = label_both) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = "black") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, size = 6), 
        legend.position = 'bottom')

```
As is expected, when we look at how forager interactions change over across climate intervals, as measured by the linear slope, there is very limited change except in the earliest intervals during which populations are being established. When changes does occur, it is primarily with agents performing directed walks and when burning costs are lower (Figure S\@ref(fig:interaction-change-over-time). 

## Relationship between forager interactions and: forager mobility and population density
Therefore, we investigate how interaction rates over time are related to mobility and population density only with directed walks using Spearman's rank correlations. 
```{r interactions-mobility, fig.cap="Relationship between proportion of population foragers interact with and steps per foraging bout at the beginning of each climatic interval across model run", echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}

Interactions are highly positively correlated with mobility throughout model run (Figure S\@ref(fig:interactions-mobility)), meaning that more mobility allows for more interactions with directed walks. 

```{r interactions-mobility-2, fig.cap="Relationship between proportion of the population foragers interact with and number of steps per foraging bout for a climatic period at the middle of model run. Relationship visualized by model scenarios with different burning costs", echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}

The strength of these correlations is impacted by burning costs. Relationship visualized by model scenarios with different burning costs", echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(rates %>% filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>%

## Maintaining connections with the same foragers
In addition to understanding overall forager interaction rates, we also loosely investigated the formation of social networks. To do so, we tracked how many of a forager's interactions during a given foraging bout overlapped with the interactions of the previous bout. Doing this provides insight into whether foragers are consistently interacting with new people or if there is incipient formation of social groups. If social groups were "forming", we would expect to see increased proportions of interactions being comprised of the same foragers. 

```{r same-network-1, fig.cap="Trends in average proportion of interactions that are the same as the previous tick across model run. Trend lines are shown for each individual climatic interval. Results shown for model scenarios with long climatic cycles (250 ticks)", echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
plot.data3 = data %>% filter(ticks > 0) %>% 
  filter(`cycle-duration` == 250) %>% 
  filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"")
plot.data3$`burn-cost` =  as.factor(plot.data3$`burn-cost`)

ggplot(plot.data3) +
  # geom_smooth(data = plot.data3, 
  #             mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, color = `burn-cost`)) +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 0 & ticks <= 250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 250 & ticks <= 500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 500 & ticks <= 750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 750 & ticks <= 1000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1000 & ticks <= 1250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1250 & ticks <= 1500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1500 & ticks <= 1750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1750 & ticks <= 2000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2000 & ticks <= 2250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2250 & ticks <= 2500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2500 & ticks <= 2750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2750 & ticks <= 3000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 3000 & ticks <= 3250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 3250 & ticks <= 3500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  #geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 2500), color = "black") +
  facet_grid(`movement-model` ~ `burn-cost`, 
             labeller = label_both, scales = "free") +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 6), 
        legend.title = element_blank(), 
        legend.position = "bottom", 
        axis.title = element_text(size = 7.5),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 7)) +
  guides(fill = "none") + 
  labs(y = "average same interaction proportion")

```

When we plot the change in average proportion of interactions that are the same as the previous tick across model run by burn cost and movement model, we see that random walks result in overall higher proportions of agents interacting with the same people compared to directed walks (Figure S\@ref(fig:same-network-1)). This is driven primarily by high rates of similar interactions in unproductive periods, particularly when burning costs are high. Conversely, with directed walks, we see an initial dip in the proportion of interactions that are with the same people as the population is establishing itself. This makes sense because the population is relatively unstable at this time, so there will be more new people on the landscape. If we consider after that burn in period, we see that the proportion of interactions that are with the same people starts to increase again and remains higher as the population reaches equilibrium and carrying capacity (Figure S\@ref(fig:same-network-1)). Because directed walks also result in fewer interactions over the course of model run, this suggests that directed walks in landscapes with a long history of burning and stable population result in smaller social networks, with foragers frequently interacting with the same people.  

# Spatial distribution of burning events  

Because burning behaviors have such a significant impact on the structure of the vegetation in the environment, we were curious if this is caused by differential use of space. To examine this, we looked at the spatial autocorrelation of where burning events occur within the landscape to assess land use by the agents.For this, we only consider significant values of Moran's I to evaluate clustering (positive values) and dispersion (negative values).

```{r burning-events-1, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%",fig.height=5}
parameters = c(
  "cycle_duration",  # 100, 250
  "veg_cycle_start", # productive, unproductive
  "veg_distribution", # random, clustered
  "burnt_neighbor_limit", # 1, 4, 8
  "burn_cost", # 0, 50
  "burn_veg_type_threshold", # 4, 7
  "movement_model" #Random, Directed
)

be.morans.100 <- readRDS("../results/outputs/be_morans.i_cycle.100.rds")
be.morans.100[,parameters[-1]] = lapply(be.morans.100[,parameters[-1]] , as.factor)
be.morans.250 <- readRDS("../results/outputs/be_morans.i_cycle.250.rds")
be.morans.250[,parameters[-1]] = lapply(be.morans.250[,parameters[-1]] , as.factor)

be.morans.100$veg_distribution = factor(be.morans.100$veg_distribution, 
                                        levels = c("\"random\"", 
                                                   "\"clustered\""))
be.morans.250$veg_distribution = factor(be.morans.250$veg_distribution, 
                                        levels = c("\"random\"", 
                                                   "\"clustered\""))

be.morans.100$movement_model = factor(be.morans.100$movement_model, 
                                      levels = c("\"Random Walk\"", 
                                                 "\"Directed Walk\""))
be.morans.250$movement_model = factor(be.morans.250$movement_model, 
                                      levels = c("\"Random Walk\"", 
                                                 "\"Directed Walk\""))

be.morans.100 = be.morans.100 %>% filter(exp %in% finished.exp)
be.morans.250 = be.morans.250 %>% filter(exp %in% finished.exp)

be.morans = bind_rows(be.morans.100, be.morans.250) %>%
  mutate(across(parameters, .fns = as.factor))

ggplot(be.morans %>% 
         filter(signif == T)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = ticks, y = morans.i, group = ticks), alpha = 0.75) +
  facet_grid(movement_model ~ veg_distribution, labeller = label_both)

```

Preliminary observation of the data shows that the different parameters show different trends in the spatial autocorrelation of burning events. Specifically we can see a trend towards dispersion when the underlying vegetation distribution is random, particularly with directed walks. We also see a trend towards highly clustered burning events when the underlying vegetation distribution is clustered; however, this effect is dampened with directed walks. To more formally investigate this, we performed an aligned ranks transformation ANOVA to statistically assess the effects of the different parameters, and their two-way interactions, on the final value of Moran's I of burning events.


```{r burning-events-1-1, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%",fig.height=4}
art_be_morans = ARTool::art(morans.i ~ cycle_duration * veg_distribution * burn_cost * burn_veg_type_threshold * burnt_neighbor_limit * movement_model, data = be.morans %>% filter(ticks == 3500))
anova_be = anova(art_be_morans)

sig_effects_be = subset(anova_be, `Pr(>F)` < 0.05)

es_be = effectsize::eta_squared(sig_effects_be, partial = T)
es_ranked_be = es_be[order(-es_be$Eta2_partial), ]
head(es_ranked_be, 10)

```

We can see that burning costs/limits still have the highest effect size on the clustering/dispersion of burning events, likely because they dictate how many burning events there will be, but after that it is underlying vegetation distribution and movement model that have the next highest effect sizes. 

```{r burning-events-2-2-2, fig.cap="Trends of spatial autocorrelation of burning events across model run for model scenarios with directed walks", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=7, out.width="100%"}
p2.2 = ggplot(be.morans.100 %>% filter(signif == T) %>% 
                filter(movement_model == "\"Directed Walk\"")) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = morans.i, 
                           color = as.factor(veg_distribution)), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = morans.i, 
                            color = as.factor(veg_distribution), 
                            group = as.factor(veg_distribution))) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0)) +
  facet_grid(burnt_neighbor_limit ~ burn_cost, 
             scales = "free", 
             labeller = labeller(burn_cost = bc.labs, 
                                 burn_veg_type_threshold = bt.labs, 
                                 burnt_neighbor_limit = bn.labs)) +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 8), 
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8), 
        legend.position = "bottom")

plot(p2.2)

```

```{r burning-events-2-2-1, fig.cap="Trends of spatial autocorrelation of burning events across model run for model scenarios with random walks", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=7, out.width="100%"}
p1.2 = ggplot(be.morans.100 %>% filter(signif == T) %>% 
                filter(movement_model == "\"Random Walk\"")) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = morans.i, 
                           color = as.factor(veg_distribution)), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = morans.i, 
                            color = as.factor(veg_distribution), 
                            group = as.factor(veg_distribution))) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0)) +
  facet_grid(burnt_neighbor_limit ~ burn_cost, 
             scales = "free", 
             labeller = labeller(burn_cost = bc.labs, 
                                 burn_veg_type_threshold = bt.labs, 
                                 burnt_neighbor_limit = bn.labs))+
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 8), 
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8), 
        legend.position = "bottom")

plot(p1.2)
```

Plotting the trends of burning event spatial autocorrelation through time by these significant parameters allows us to better visualize these patterns. Here, we split the data by movement model with trends for directed walks (Figure S\@ref(fig:burning-events-2-2-2)) and trend lines for random walks (Figure S\@ref(fig:burning-events-2-2-1)). 

First, it is clear that, under random walks, underlying distribution of vegetation potential has a significant impact on clustering or disperson of burning events (Figure S\@ref(fig:burning-events-2-2-1)). This is especially true when burning is limited to specific patches under low burning costs. As burning costs increase, and burning becomes more infrequent, burning events are more likely to cluster despite limits on which patches can be burnt. 

With directed walks, the effect of underlying vegetation potential is more varied (Figure S\@ref(fig:burning-events-2-2-2)). For example, when agents can burn any vegetation type, underlying vegetation potential does not change the trend towards spatial randomness or dispersion of burning events. When agents can only burn specific vegetation types, underlying vegetation potential is more important, particularly in cases where patches can have more burnt neighbors. In these cases, underlying clustering of vegetation type potential leads to more clustering of burning events.
